Chapter 3: The Power of Naming Emotions and Practicing Self-Compassion
Now that we’ve explored the emotional roots behind procrastination, let’s talk about something that can really change the game—managing those feelings when they show up. One of the best ways to do this? Simply name what you’re feeling when you’re about to avoid a tough task.
It might sound almost too simple, but naming your emotions is surprisingly powerful. Say you notice, “I’m anxious about starting this report,” or, “I feel overwhelmed by this project.” By labeling the feeling, it suddenly feels a bit less overwhelming, right? It’s like you’re shining a flashlight into a dark room—the shadows don’t seem so scary, and you can see what’s really going on.
When you acknowledge your emotions in this way, they become a lot more manageable. Instead of reacting on autopilot, you give yourself the space to respond thoughtfully. The urge to avoid starts to lose its grip.
But there’s another tool that’s just as important—self-compassion. It’s so common to beat ourselves up when we procrastinate, thinking that a little tough love will whip us into shape. But honestly, that kind of self-criticism usually backfires. The more we’re harsh with ourselves, the more stress and shame we pile on, and the harder it gets to even start.
Self-compassion is about treating yourself like you would a good friend. That means recognizing that everyone puts things off sometimes, and that it’s a totally normal part of being human—not some big personal failing.
And here’s something worth remembering: research shows that people who forgive themselves for procrastinating are actually less likely to put things off again. Self-forgiveness breaks that cycle of guilt and avoidance, and suddenly, there’s room to build new habits.
Imagine a student who misses a study session. It’s easy to slip into, “I’ll never get this right.” But with a little self-compassion, it might sound more like, “You know, I had a tough day, and it was hard to focus. I can try again tomorrow.” That gentle response lowers the shame and makes it so much easier to get back on track.
So, what can this look like day to day? Here are a few simple ways to start:
Take a pause and ask yourself, “What am I feeling right now?”
Give that emotion a name—maybe it’s anxiety, frustration, or even boredom.
And then, offer yourself a kind response, like, “It’s okay to feel this way. I can start small.”
When you combine emotional awareness with self-compassion, you break the link between tough feelings and avoidance. That’s how you start building real, lasting change—approaching tasks with more confidence, and a lot more resilience.
